intro: At midnight on a budget deadline, national parks lock their gates and passport offices stop answering, while Social Security checks keep going out. In a grocery aisle in Chicago, a carton of eggs costs three times what it did two years before, and no one in the store set the price. These two scenes come from different halves of this unit, government and economics, but they share one lesson. The rules that run a country are not the short text of the Constitution or a diagram of supply and demand. They are hundreds of practical arrangements, built over two centuries, that decide who actually gets to choose and who pays for the choice.

The first chapter follows the three branches as they really work: the committee chair who never schedules a hearing, the sixty-vote Senate, the president who acts by executive order and the court that reads the same words two ways. It comes home to Illinois, with its 1970 constitution and nearly seven thousand local governments, and to the contested machinery of elections, from campaign money to district maps to the Electoral College. The second chapter turns to the economy: scarcity and incentives, prices and competition, the failures that justify rules, the numbers that describe a nation's health, the levers Congress and the Federal Reserve pull, the effects of trade, and the choices you will make with your own paycheck, credit card and college application.

By the end you should be able to trace how a bill, a budget, a court case or an interest-rate change actually moves through the system, to explain why a price rose using evidence rather than blame, and to judge a claim about either government or the economy by asking who made it, what others found and whether the numbers support it. These are the skills of a citizen who cannot be easily fooled, and they are the point of the unit.
bigQuestion: In a country where no single person runs the government or sets prices, who really decides, what limits them, and how can a citizen tell a good decision from a bad one?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, describing self-interest and markets
The Constitution gives Congress the power to tax, borrow, coin money and regulate trade
Marbury v. Madison establishes judicial review
The Chicago Board of Trade opens, becoming the price-setting market for Midwestern grain
The Pendleton Act begins filling federal jobs by merit rather than party loyalty
The Sherman Antitrust Act outlaws restraint of trade and monopolizing
Congress creates the Federal Reserve after the Panic of 1907
Unemployment reaches about one in four workers at the depth of the Great Depression
Youngstown Sheet and Tube v. Sawyer limits presidential power against Congress's will
Illinois adopts its current state constitution
The housing crash produces the deepest recession since the 1930s
Pandemic shutdown, two trillion dollars in relief, nine percent inflation and the fastest rate hikes in forty years

words.d: a small group of members of Congress that studies, rewrites and can kill a bill before the full chamber votes
the Senate practice of extending debate so a bill needs sixty votes to move forward
a directive from the president to the executive branch that has the force of law without a vote of Congress
the power of courts to strike down laws and government actions that conflict with the Constitution
drawing election district lines to favor one party or group
the value of the next-best option given up when a choice is made
the price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer
a cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on someone who was not part of it
a general rise in prices across the economy, which lowers what each dollar buys
Congress's use of spending and taxes to influence the economy
the Federal Reserve's use of interest rates to steer the economy toward stable prices and full employment
a tax on imported goods, which raises their price to protect domestic producers

test.q: Where does most of the real work of shaping a bill in Congress happen?
choices: In committees
On the floor of the full House
In the Supreme Court
In the president's cabinet
test.why: Committees hold hearings, rewrite bills and decide which ones ever reach a vote.

test.q: Why does a Senate majority of fifty-three often fail to pass a major bill?
choices: The president can refuse to sign
The House must approve first
Ending a filibuster requires sixty votes
The Constitution requires two-thirds for all laws
test.why: Cloture, the vote to end debate, needs sixty senators, so a simple majority is usually not enough.

test.q: In a government shutdown, which of these continues?
choices: Processing new passport applications
Guided tours at national parks
Most federal grant reviews
Social Security payments
test.why: Mandatory spending set by permanent law keeps flowing; discretionary services that need a yearly appropriation stop.

test.q: Under Justice Jackson's test from the 1952 steel seizure case, when is a president's power weakest?
choices: When acting with Congress's approval
When Congress has said nothing
When acting against Congress's expressed will
During wartime
test.why: Truman lost because Congress had considered and rejected giving presidents the power to seize industries.

test.q: What power did Marbury v. Madison establish in 1803?
choices: The president's veto
The Senate filibuster
The Fed's control of interest rates
Courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution
test.why: Chief Justice Marshall claimed for the courts the duty to say what the law is, which is judicial review.

test.q: How do Illinois Supreme Court justices differ from federal judges?
choices: Illinois justices are elected by district to ten-year terms
Illinois justices are appointed for life
Illinois justices are chosen by the U.S. president
There is no difference
test.why: Federal judges are appointed for life; Illinois voters elect their justices by district.

test.q: A party with a minority of a state's voters wins most of its districts by packing the other party's voters into a few districts. What is this?
choices: The Electoral College
Gerrymandering
The rule of four
Cloture
test.why: Packing and cracking voters across district lines to win more seats than votes would justify is gerrymandering.

test.q: The opportunity cost of a free concert ticket is best described as what?
choices: Zero, because the ticket was free
The price other people paid
The best thing you could have done with that evening instead
The cost of the bus ride
test.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative given up, which exists even when no money changes hands.

test.q: Bird flu kills tens of millions of hens. What happens in the egg market and why?
choices: Price falls because demand drops
Price stays fixed because stores set it
Price rises because supply falls while demand stays about the same
Supply rises to replace the lost hens immediately
test.why: A supply shock with steady demand raises the price until enough buyers drop out and farms rebuild flocks.

test.q: Why do governments usually pay for national defense and lighthouses with taxes?
choices: Because they are public goods that free riders would use without paying
Because they are monopolies
Because they are externalities
Because private companies are banned from building them
test.why: A public good cannot be withheld from those who do not pay, so private sellers will not supply enough of it.

test.q: What is the difference between fiscal policy and monetary policy?
choices: Fiscal policy is state; monetary policy is federal
Fiscal policy is Congress's taxing and spending; monetary policy is the Fed's control of interest rates
Fiscal policy controls trade; monetary policy controls prices
They are two names for the same thing
test.why: Congress holds the budget levers under Article I; the Federal Reserve sets interest rates.

test.q: Between 2022 and 2023 the Federal Reserve raised interest rates from near zero to over five percent. What was it trying to do?
choices: Increase the national debt
Raise exports
Create a recession on purpose
Slow spending to bring down nine percent inflation
test.why: Higher borrowing costs cool spending across the economy, which was the Fed's tool against the 2022 inflation.

test.q: Which best describes the national debt by 2025?
choices: Roughly equal to a year of GDP, with interest taking about one federal dollar in eight
Fully paid off after the pandemic
Owed entirely to China
Smaller than the yearly deficit
test.why: The debt passed thirty-six trillion dollars, near the size of annual GDP, and interest costs exceeded military spending.

test.q: A tariff on imported steel is imposed. Which group is most likely to lose?
choices: Steelworkers at a protected mill
Companies that make cans and cars from steel, and farmers hit by retaliation
The Federal Reserve
Foreign steel buyers
test.why: Tariffs raise costs for industries that buy the protected product and invite retaliation against exporters like Illinois soybean farmers.

test.q: A political ad shows a chart of one city's crime rising in a single year and blames the mayor. What is the best first step in evaluating it?
choices: Share it if you agree with it
Assume it is false because it is an ad
Check the source, compare other cities and the years left out, and see whether the evidence supports the claim
Ask whether the mayor is popular
test.why: Evaluating a claim means checking who made it, what others found and whether the data actually support the conclusion.

write.prompt: The federal government put a twenty-five percent tariff on imported steel in 2018. Take a position: should Illinois's senators have supported it? Make a claim, support it with evidence from this unit about how tariffs work, who gained and lost in Illinois, and how Congress actually decides, then explain your reasoning and answer the strongest argument on the other side.
tips: Claim: state clearly whether the tariff was worth its costs for Illinois, not just for one town.
Evidence: use the Granite City mill, the Decatur soybean farmers, the can makers, the federal farm payments and the Sherman Act idea of competition.
Reasoning: connect each piece of evidence to the claim using opportunity cost, comparative advantage or incentives.
The other side: name the best argument against you, such as saved jobs or lower prices, and explain why your evidence outweighs it.
Process: mention how a senator would actually act on this, through committees, votes and the sixty-vote Senate.
